label: Officer Was Not Lawfully Present When the Item Was Seen (Not Plain View)
motion_heading: The Plain-View Doctrine Does Not Apply Because the Officer Was Not Lawfully in the Place From Which the Item Was Seen

sentences.text: The plain-view doctrine permits a warrantless seizure only if the officer did not violate the Fourth Amendment in arriving at the place from which the object could be plainly viewed.
The officer must also have a lawful right of access to the object itself.

practice_notes: This issue usually depends on another one: if the entry, stop, or search that put the officer there was unlawful, plain view falls with it. Make sure that underlying issue is argued too.
_author_notes: REVIEW CAREFULLY (legal judgment not yet reviewed): this issue is suggested when the officer was somewhere private (inside a vehicle, the yard, inside a building, or somewhere else) with no stated reason for being there, or had a warrant or consent but went beyond it. A public place, outside a vehicle looking in, and the front door (an ordinary knock-and-talk) don't suggest it; nor do a warrant, consent, an emergency, or an arrest. Those can still be challenged as their own issues. Drafted by Claude on 2026-10-12 and built at the maintainer's request; not yet legally agreed.
